newsitem.title: CHINA: Brittan says gains China backing on WTO.
newsitem.headline: Brittan says gains China backing on WTO.

text.p: China has pledged support for phased acceptance of obligations in order to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Friday.

Brittan told reporters the assurances were given to him by senior Chinese officials, and he would now seek U.S. backing for efforts to push forward China's long-stalled plan to join the global trade organisation.
Brittan said he would relay the Chinese position to U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher who is scheduled to visit Beijing next week.
"It was necessary to check that the Chinese support the phased acceptance of the obligations... That was confirmed very strongly and very warmly ...," Brittan said.

"I am now urgently getting in touch with the United States and Secretary of State Warren Christopher before his arrival here in Beijing to urge that we work together to accelerate Chinese participation in the WTO," he said.
Beijing wants to join the WTO on the lenient terms of a developing country but the U.S. has resisted, saying that China's economy is too big.
Europe has said it would be flexible if Beijing accepted some obligations initially and supported full compliance eventually.
Brittan, who is currently in Beijing leading a European trade delegation, described China as needing to make a "down payment" on WTO terms with full compliance later.
He said the assurances of acceptance of the European position were given to him by Vice Premier Zhu Rongji and Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi.
He also said that China's WTO drive would be taken up at a bilateral meeting in January and that the European team would be larger and more senior than originally planned.
On Thursday, China's trade minister Wu expressed doubt that the United States would be willing to change its tough stance on Beijing's proposed admission to WTO.
But the European official said that the end of the U.S. presidential election campaign could be an opportunity for making progress in the negotiations.
He also warned that Europe would not be discriminated against in the Chinese market.

He singled out as an area of concern a June agreement with two U.S. shipping companies, allowing them to set up wholly owned freight forwarders. Companies from other countries would not have this right for three years.
Separately, China said that Sino-European Union (EU) trade was facing challenges from EU anti-dumping measures and quota restrictions against Chinese exports.
The official Xinhua news agency said that since 1990, the EU had lodged 35 anti-dumping cases against China.
The most recent case was an anti-dumping investigation aimed at Chinese textile exports to the EU.
"Such discriminatory measures and unfair practices will seriously hinder the growth of Sino-EU trade ties if they are not corrected at an early date," the agency said.
